title: Rituximab (monoclonal anti-CD20 antibody) induced posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES): A case report and literature review
case_prompt:
A 23-year-old woman with an 8-year history of systemic lupus erythematosus and lupus nephritis presented after four generalized tonic-clonic seizures accompanied by severe headaches, visual disturbances, and altered mental status. Two days before her first seizure, she had developed moderate occipital headaches, and 6 hours before the seizures she noted declining vision. She received her first dose of rituximab 5 days earlier for refractory lupus nephritis and a second dose before hospital discharge; visual blurring and retro-orbital pain began acutely after the second dose. On examination she was listless, confused, and intermittently seizing; neurological examination showed bilateral cortical blindness and hyperreflexia. Glasgow Coma Scale scores fluctuated between 5 and 9. Vital signs were within normal limits. Complete blood count, electrolytes, and renal function tests were unremarkable. 

Emergency brain MRI revealed multifocal, asymmetrical hypointensities on T1-weighted images and corresponding hyperintensities on T2-weighted and FLAIR sequences involving subcortical U-fibers and deep white and gray matter in bilateral frontal, parietal, temporal, and occipital lobes (predominant in occipital lobes), bilateral thalami, gangliocapsular regions, corona radiata, centrum semiovale, hemipons, middle cerebellar peduncles, and cerebellar hemispheres, with mild vasogenic edema and effacement of adjacent sulci. DWI showed few areas of patchy reduced diffusivity; SWI demonstrated no susceptibility artifacts.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Ischemic stroke was considered but the imaging demonstrated widespread vasogenic edema rather than the cytotoxic edema typical of infarction — “the characteristic imaging findings on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) include symmetric hyperintensities on T2-weighted and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) sequences, indicative of vasogenic edema.”  
2. Central nervous system infection was in the differential, but there were no systemic or laboratory signs of infection — “the differential diagnosis for PRES includes infections of the central nervous system.”  
3. Intracerebral hemorrhage was excluded by the absence of blood-sensitive signals on susceptibility-weighted imaging — “SWI: no susceptibility artifacts.”  
4. Demyelinating disease, such as multiple sclerosis, was less likely given the acute, diffuse, reversible subcortical vasogenic edema in the posterior regions — “differential diagnosis for PRES includes … demyelinating diseases (like multiple sclerosis).”  
5. Drug-induced PRES was suspected based on the temporal association with rituximab administration and clinical-imaging findings of reversible posterior vasogenic edema — “an increasing number of cases have been reported in association with monoclonal anti-CD20 antibody therapies, including Rituximab.”
